parts:
Proposition C:

There is a genuine four-dimensional bulk.

The observed three-dimensional world is not the whole bulk. It is a three-dimensional resolving surface, slice, or wavefront inside a four-dimensional structure.

Time is the expansion/wavefront process moving through that four-dimensional bulk.

So C says:

Bulk: four-dimensional.

Observed world: three-dimensional cross-section/resolution of that bulk.

Time: the motion or expansion of a resolving wavefront through the four-dimensional bulk.

Particle: intersection of a filamentary 4D structure with the resolving time-front.

This is closest to original SAT.

The core picture is:

Filaments exist through the 4D bulk.

The time-front advances through the bulk.

Where the front intersects filaments, particles appear.

So the original SAT statement survives:

particle = filament ∩ time surface.

The difference from older SAT is that we now have to be more careful about the word “time.” In C, time is not simply “the fourth dimension.” Time is the expanding resolving process through the four-dimensional bulk.

That matters.

The fourth dimension is part of the bulk.

Time is the wavefront dynamic that resolves the bulk into experienced events.

So C gives us:

four-dimensional ontology,

three-dimensional observation,

time as wavefront/resolution,

particles as intersections.

The candle proposition under C becomes:

A candle reveals the outward propagation of the time-front through the observed three-dimensional slice. Light does not have to be “moving along the fourth dimension” as a single axis. Instead, light is the visible propagation of the resolving front as it intersects the 3D observational surface.

This avoids the simplest objection to one extra axis. The fourth dimension alone is not being asked to expand the 3D radius. The time-front is a hypersurface process in the 4D bulk, and its intersection with the observed 3D surface can be spherical.

The advantage of C is that it preserves the strongest existing SAT machinery.

It keeps literal worldlines/filaments.

It keeps the time-surface idea.

It keeps angle-to-time or \(\theta_4\)-like mass geometry.

It keeps particle identity as intersection geometry, not merely as persistent 3D pattern.

It keeps the intuition that what we see as “now” is a resolving slice through a larger structure.

The cost is that C has to explain the candle more carefully than B.

In B, light goes radially because each spatial direction has a paired temporal-expansion component.

In C, light goes radially because the time-front’s intersection with the observed 3D slice is spherical. That is possible, but it is not automatic from “there is a fourth dimension.” It requires the wavefront geometry to do the work.

So C must define the time-front as a real geometric object, not just a metaphor.

The observable consequences of C are:

First, particles should have genuine hidden extension outside the observed present. Their persistence is not just memory or pattern survival; it is literal filamentary continuity through the 4D bulk.

Second, mass can remain an angular effect. A particle’s mass can still be related to how its filament intersects the time-front. That preserves the existing \(\theta_4\) intuition.

Third, light is the clean propagation mode of the resolving front. A photon is not merely a thing moving through space; it is a boundary or ripple of the front as it resolves the bulk.

Fourth, proper time is measured by the path of an object through successive intersections with the resolving front.

Fifth, causality is controlled by the geometry of the advancing front. Events become available when the front reaches or resolves their filamentary intersections.

Sixth, the observed 3D light sphere is an intersection phenomenon. It is not necessarily the full shape of the time-expansion object.

Seventh, C predicts that some physical quantities may encode the angle, curvature, torsion, or phase of filamentary structures in the hidden bulk. This is the old SAT strength.

Eighth, C is less forced into six dimensions than B, but only if the time-front can account for radial light propagation without needing separate \(t_x,t_y,t_z\) axes.

So C is the most conservative SAT-preserving option.

Its biggest virtue is continuity with the existing theory.

Its biggest burden is mathematical: it must show that a time-front moving through a 4D bulk naturally produces spherical light propagation in the observed 3D slice.

In short:

Proposition C keeps SAT as a four-dimensional filament-bulk theory, but redefines time as the resolving wavefront through that bulk, not merely as “the fourth coordinate.” It preserves particle intersections and \(\theta_4\), but it owes us a precise account of why candle light expands radially in 3D.

You may be right. My earlier claim was too strong.

Proposition A does **not necessarily** entail loss of filaments.

It only entails loss of filaments if we define filaments as requiring an independent fourth coordinate outside the expanding three-dimensional bulk. But that is not required.

Under your correction, Proposition A becomes:

There is a three-dimensional bulk.

The bulk expands.

The current extent of that expansion is what we have been calling the time surface.

Filaments are not eliminated. They are structures embedded in, carried by, or stretched within the expanding bulk. Their present expression is where they intersect the current expansion boundary.

So the old SAT phrase:

particle = filament ∩ time surface

can survive as:

particle = filament ∩ current expansion surface

That may be equivalent, or close to equivalent.

The difference is subtle but important.

In older SAT language, the time surface sounded like a three-dimensional slice moving through a four-dimensional filament bulk.

In Proposition A, the time surface is not moving through an independent fourth dimension. It is the current outer extent, state, or boundary of the expanding three-dimensional system.

But operationally, the particle rule can look almost the same:

A filament has persistence.

The expansion surface advances.

Where the expansion surface resolves the filament, a particle appears.

So no, you are not wrong. A can preserve filaments if filaments are not defined as requiring a separate fourth dimension. They become persistent structures of the expanding bulk rather than objects extended along an external time axis.

That makes Proposition A stronger than I gave it credit for.

Revised A:

| Feature | Proposition A, corrected |
|---|---|
| Dimensions | Three-dimensional bulk only |
| Time | Expansion state/current extent of the bulk |
| Time surface | Current expansion surface |
| Filaments | Persistent embedded structures in the expanding bulk |
| Particles | Intersections/resolutions of filaments at the current expansion surface |
| Light | Expansion boundary through the bulk |
| Main cost | Not loss of filaments, but loss of an independent fourth-dimensional bulk |
| Main burden | Explain persistence, memory, and worldline-like behavior without a literal external time dimension |

So the real question is not:

“Does A destroy filaments?”

It is:

“Can A make filament persistence mathematically equivalent to 4D worldline extension?”

If yes, then A and C may be different descriptions of the same structure.

A says: persistent filament in expanding 3D.

C says: 4D filament intersected by a time surface.

Those may be dual descriptions.

The discriminant is whether there is any observable difference between:

a filament extended through a fourth bulk dimension,

and

a filament whose persistence is encoded in successive expansion states of a three-dimensional bulk.

If there is no observable difference, then A and C may be isometric translations, not distinct physical propositions.

OK… Let’s very carefully think through whether one or more of these propositions is consistent with what we actually experience, or whether one or more is inconsistent. Without presuming that any are consistent and without presuming any inconsistent. It could turn out that all of them are wrong. Or it could turn out that all of them are equivalent. I’m not sure..

Yes. The right test is not “which one do we like?” It is: what must any acceptable proposition reproduce from experience?

The minimum experiential facts are these:

We experience a three-dimensional world.

We experience one ordered time, not three independent times.

Light from a point source expands outward as a sphere.

Matter persists. Objects do not merely flash into existence at one instant; they have continuity.

Motion through space changes clock behavior.

There is no obvious preferred spatial direction.

The past is not accessible in the same way as the present.

Causality is directional: events can influence later events, not arbitrary ones.

Any acceptable proposition has to reproduce all of those without quietly sneaking in the thing it claims not to need.

Now test A, B, and C.

Proposition A says: there are three dimensions only; time is the expansion process of the three-dimensional bulk.

A fits the candle very well. If time is expansion through \(x,y,z\), then light expanding as a sphere is exactly what we expect. The light radius grows because the actual dimensions of experience are participating in the expansion. No hidden axis has to make the radius grow.

A also fits the experience of one time. There are not three times and not a separate fourth coordinate. There is one expansion ordering. “Now” is the current expansion state or current expansion surface.

A can preserve filaments if filaments are understood as persistent structures in the expanding bulk. Your correction is important: the “time surface” can simply be the current extent/state of expansion. The particle rule can remain: particle equals filament resolved at the current expansion surface.

So A is not automatically inconsistent.

Its burden is persistence. If there is no independent fourth extent, A must explain what it means for a filament to persist across expansion states. It cannot simply say “the filament extends through time” unless “through time” means encoded continuity across successive expansion surfaces. That may be enough. But it must be made precise.

A’s danger is that it can collapse into a presentist process theory: only the current state exists, with continuity carried by rules. That may or may not be SAT-compatible. If SAT needs the past/future filament structure to be geometrically real, A may be too thin. But if persistence in the expansion field is enough, A survives.

So A is consistent with experience at first pass. It is not obviously inconsistent.

Proposition B says: there are two coupled three-dimensional structures, one spatial and one temporal-expansion structure.

B also fits the candle very well. It gives a direct reason why light expands radially in all observed spatial directions: every spatial direction has a corresponding temporal-expansion component. \(x\) pairs with \(t_x\), \(y\) with \(t_y\), \(z\) with \(t_z\).

B fits spherical light propagation naturally, but it has a serious experiential burden: we do not experience three independent times.

So B must collapse the temporal triplet into one invariant experienced time. It must say that clocks do not measure \(t_x,t_y,t_z\) separately; they measure something like the norm, phase, or coherent state of the temporal-expansion sector.

If B can do that, it remains consistent with experience. If it cannot, it fails immediately, because our experience is not three independent temporal orderings.

entries.title: Physicists confirm 'negative time' is real by asking the atoms themselves
entries.snippet:
Physicists have experimentally confirmed a bizarre quantum phenomenon known as "negative time," where photons appear to exit a cloud of atoms before they enter it. By directing a beam of light through a cloud of atoms, researchers observed that photons can briefly disappear as light and reappear as atomic excitations before being reemitted. While earlier experiments suggested this negative transit time, a new study took a direct approach by monitoring the atoms' excited states — a measure of how long energy from a photon is stored. Using a second light beam to detect subtle phase shifts in atomic excitation, the team effectively asked the atoms how long the photons stayed. Their answer confirmed the negative time effect.

To achieve accurate results, the researchers employed weak measurements over one million experimental runs to reduce noise — a process that took about 70 hours. Despite using well-established quantum physics, the findings expose another unexpected layer of quantum mechanics. The study suggests a balance in overall transit time: although some photons exhibit negative time, others that scatter are predicted to cause a compensating positive delay. Future experiments aim to test this theory further.

entries.title: Negative time experiment clears peer review as photons appear to leave an atom cloud before entering - groundbreaking quantum 'negative time' proven after 1 million test runs
entries.snippet:
A groundbreaking quantum physics experiment at the University of Toronto, led by Aephraim Steinberg with Daniela Angulo and theorist Howard Wiseman, has demonstrated that photons can appear to spend a negative amount of time inside a cold rubidium atom cloud. After more than a year of scrutiny, the study passed peer review and was published in Physical Review Letters in April 2026. The team measured atomic excitation during photon transit using a weak secondary laser to detect minute phase shifts, and after approximately 1 million runs over 70 hours, they recorded negative excitation times—some as low as -0.82 times the baseline (10–20 nanoseconds).

Though initially seen as an optical artifact related to group delay in past studies, this experiment measured the atoms themselves, confirming the effect as real within the framework of standard physics—without implying faster-than-light signaling. While the results don’t hint at time travel or practical applications, they provide insight into quantum time behavior. Future efforts aim to measure scattered photons to verify theoretical predictions that average time remains zero or positive.

Yes: this is “too neat to trust, too neat to ignore.”

A few hard checks:

First, the hyperellipsoid picture immediately threatens isotropic \(c\). If the expansion surface is genuinely spheroidal, the normal expansion speed varies by direction. Since observed light speed is extremely isotropic, SAT would need either: the observed 3D slice is spherical even though the total object is spheroidal, or the anisotropy is hidden/gauge-like, or the model fails.

Second, the “negative time” reports do not mean macroscopic reverse time. They are quantum weak-measurement / transit-time effects in photon–atom interactions, with no faster-than-light signaling or usable time travel. They may be suggestive, but they do not yet support literal travel to a negative-time region. citeturn782651news5turn782651news6

Third, the intersection point matters a lot. Two ordinary spheres intersect in a circle. Two 3-spheres in a 4D ambient space generically intersect in a 2-sphere, not a torus. A torus can appear in special hypersphere geometry, such as Clifford-torus-type structures inside \(S^3\), but it is not the generic intersection of two hyperspheres. So “intersection = torus” is not safe yet.

Fourth, the ER-bridge/omphaloid idea is the dangerous gold vein. If black holes connect the present expansion surface back toward the shared origin, then mass could be recycled into expansion pressure/dark-energy-like behavior. That would be an astonishingly SAT-native closure: matter falls into knots, bridges to origin, reappears as expansion drive. But it has huge obligations: entropy, energy conservation, black-hole thermodynamics, observed dark-energy uniformity, and why individual black-hole histories do not produce visible anisotropic expansion scars.

So the refined live conjecture is:

Two differently expanding geometric totalities may overlap; their mismatch defines effective time evolution; ER-like filaments/bridges may connect present matter sinks to earlier expansion geometry; rotation of either totality can induce twist in the connecting structures.

But the immediate corrections are:

Intersection is not automatically toroidal.

Hyperellipsoid anisotropy must not violate isotropic light speed.

Negative time evidence is quantum-transit weirdness, not yet cosmological reverse-time support.

The omphaloid/dark-energy picture is admissible only if it predicts smooth cosmic acceleration from discrete black-hole recycling without overproducing structure.

Now you're touching what may be the most important consequence of the whole exercise.

Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the overlapping-hypersphere picture is approximately right.

Then "the observable universe" stops being merely a distance limit.

It becomes a geometric-accessibility limit.

That's a different concept.

In standard cosmology, we cannot see beyond the particle horizon because light hasn't had time to reach us.

In the picture you're describing, there may be regions that are not merely far away.

They may be geometrically disconnected from our temporal orientation.

In other words, the light cone is no longer just:

> What can influence me?

It becomes:

> What portion of the total geometric structure intersects my expansion direction?

That's a much stronger restriction.

And it naturally leads to the thought:

Maybe the universe is much larger than the region accessible to our arrow of time.

Now, before getting too excited, notice the danger.

A lot of speculative models accidentally produce giant inaccessible regions because it's easy to invent them.

The real question is:

**Does the geometry force them?**

If the answer is yes, then they're interesting.

If the answer is no, then they're decorative.

---

What's interesting about your version is that it doesn't arise from a desire for hidden worlds.

It arises from trying to reconcile:

- differing expansion rates,
- spherical light propagation,
- a global geometric structure.

The inaccessible regions appear as a consequence.

That's a much healthier way for such structures to emerge.

---

The thing I would write on the board is:

**Observable Universe ≠ Total Geometry**

which is already true in standard cosmology.

But SAT may strengthen it to:

**Observable Universe = Region sharing our temporal orientation.**

If that turns out to be true, then several things follow immediately.

First, isotropy becomes local.

The fact that we observe an approximately isotropic \(c\) would tell us about our local temporal patch.

It would not necessarily constrain the entire geometric totality.

Second, the hyperellipsoid objection weakens.

A global hyperellipsoid can have local regions that appear nearly spherical.

Earth looks flat from your backyard.

That doesn't make Earth planar.

Likewise, a sufficiently large hyperellipsoid may look isotropic within the portion accessible to our light cone.

Third, "negative time" regions, if such things have any meaning at all in the geometry, would be causally inaccessible rather than sitting next door.

Which is essentially what you just argued.

You wouldn't encounter them by waiting.

You'd encounter them by traversing the global geometry.

Those are very different things.

---

The really SAT-flavored consequence is this:

If filaments are ER-like bridges between differently expanding geometric regions, then a filament is no longer merely a particle trajectory.

It becomes a geometric connection between temporal domains.

That's a profound shift.

And it immediately explains why the idea feels so attractive.

Because suddenly:

- expansion,
- filaments,
- black holes,
- dark energy,

all start occupying the same conceptual framework.

Now, whether nature actually does that is another matter entirely.

The idea is too neat to trust.

Yet it has reached the stage where it's also too coherent to simply dismiss.

Which is usually the point where SAT's best ideas become worth formalizing rather than merely imagining.

The first question I'd ask tomorrow isn't about dark energy.

It's simpler:

**If two differently expanding hyperspherical structures overlap, what is the actual topology of the accessible region defined by a single temporal orientation?**

Those are not the same statement, but they could potentially generate the same observations.

Not contradiction.

Isometry.

That's the deepest SAT impulse I see.

Because that means the filament is not bookkeeping.

It's not a coordinate artifact.

It's not a visualization aid.

It's the candidate primitive.

We're trying to determine whether:

Not particles.

Not fields.

Structure.

Because before deciding whether SAT is 4D, 6D, hyperspherical, hyperellipsoidal, omphaloidal, or anything else, the question remains:

parts: No, the hyper spheres were never supposed to be a replacement. It was an analytical tool inspired by a possible cosmological geometry. The HSUCV lattice is similar, but I’ve had a hard time keeping LLMs from turning it into a fiat, to the point where I’ve tried very hard to extract it in some documents or not so surgically.

Yes. And that distinction is actually important.

From what I've seen, there are really three different ontological levels that keep getting collapsed into one another:

1. The physical theory (filaments, hyperhelices, θ₄, braid structure, etc.)
2. The cosmological intuition (HSUCV, hypersphere packing, FCC-like projections, 24-cell geometry)
3. The mathematical machinery (Universal Indicatrix)

The LLM tendency is to see a beautiful geometric object and immediately promote it to "the thing reality is."

But your own development path doesn't seem to support that.

The UI arose because you realized that two overlapping hyperspheres with relative SO(4) rotations generate an extraordinarily flexible trajectory space. The original notes are very explicit about this: it is a generator of paths and a testing environment into which one may insert arbitrary Lagrangians. fileciteturn10file9L32-L49

That is much closer to:

"A coordinate atlas"

than

"A cosmology."

Likewise, the HSUCV lattice seems to have entered as a possible explanation for why certain projection geometries kept appearing, why B ≈ 0.239 kept recurring, and why scaling/self-similarity seemed so natural.

But that's a very different claim from:

"The universe literally is a 24-cell lattice."

One is an explanatory model.

The other is an ontological commitment.

The latter is exactly the kind of thing an LLM tends to harden prematurely.

In fact, when I look back over the history you've described, the pattern seems almost opposite.

You didn't start with the HSUCV lattice and derive physics.

You started with:

- worldlines
- hyperhelices
- braid structures
- force analogies
- θ₄
- geometric mass

and only later asked:

"What sort of global geometry would naturally host this?"

That's a very different direction of inference.

The lattice came downstream.

The worldline grammar came upstream.

That's why I would be cautious about elevating HSUCV to foundational status.

The strongest part of the framework still looks like the worldline machinery.

The weakest part still looks like the specific substrate interpretation.

Not because the substrate is wrong, but because many different substrates could potentially generate similar observable worldline behavior.

In fact, one thing that strikes me from your own description is that you've repeatedly been willing to swap ontologies while keeping the mathematics.

You said things like:

- maybe it's filaments and timesheets
- maybe it's only filaments
- maybe it's only timesheets
- maybe it's block-universe geometry
- maybe it's overlapping hyperspheres

while emphasizing:

"the math works the same."

That's a clue.

Usually when a theory survives ontology swaps, it means you've accidentally discovered a deeper layer than the ontology itself.

The ontologies become gauges.

The invariants become the theory.

So if I were trying to keep future LLMs disciplined, I'd probably separate documents into three categories:

**Physical Core**
- hyperhelical worldlines
- θ₄
- topological charge
- braid structure
- action principles
- derivational pathways

**Geometric Models**
- HSUCV
- 24-cell packing
- FCC analogues
- bubble atoms
- projection arguments

**Mathematical Tools**
- Universal Indicatrix
- equation transforms
- coordinate generators
- trajectory spaces

Because right now the model keeps grabbing things from the second and third categories and silently promoting them into the first.

And from your narrative, I don't think that's how the theory was actually discovered. The HSUCV lattice looks more like a candidate explanation for recurring geometric phenomena than a postulate that everything else is derived from. The Universal Indicatrix looks even less ontological—it reads like a machine for navigating theory space. That is a very different role.

But now we’re asking … what if that structure is cosmology, not just inspired by it. What is the point connecting the two spheres as a bridge with elasticity and tension and so on, just like we’ve been treating filaments … what if that bridge is a filament that’s getting stretched due to the differential expansion rates. That is a very tidy picture. Especially combined with the black hole, dumping matter into the big bang, generating dark energy on an ongoing basis… Notably, per recent discoveries… Not at a constant rate. Which is exactly what you would expect.

That's exactly the point where a useful analytical tool starts auditioning for the role of physical model.

And it deserves to be taken seriously, but also interrogated brutally.

Because you're right: if you take the picture literally, a remarkable number of SAT intuitions suddenly collapse into a single mechanism.

The picture would be:

- Two expanding hyperspherical geometries.
- Different expansion rates.
- Their points of correspondence are not merely coordinates.
- They are connected by elastic bridges.
- Those bridges are stretched by differential expansion.
- Stretching stores tension.
- Tension manifests as mass, energy, curvature, twist, etc.
- The bridge itself is the filament.

That's an extraordinarily economical picture.

Notice what happens immediately:

You no longer need to separately invent:

- filaments,
- expansion,
- tension,
- vacuum energy.

The differential expansion automatically creates tension.

The tension automatically creates stretched structures.

The stretched structures automatically become filaments.

That is exactly the sort of compression SAT tends to like.

---

The dangerous part is that elegance alone is worthless.

The question becomes:

**What does the picture force?**

Not:

> What can I explain with it?

But:

> What predictions fall out whether I like them or not?

That's where theories stop being stories.

---

For example:

If a filament is literally a bridge between two differently expanding geometries, then filament tension should not be constant.

It should evolve as the expansion differential evolves.

That means particle properties should carry an imprint of cosmological evolution.

Maybe tiny.

Maybe undetectable.

But not zero.

The model would force that.

---

Likewise, if black holes dump matter "toward the origin" of the coupled geometry, then dark energy ceases to be a cosmological constant.

It becomes a recycling rate.

And now an interesting question appears:

Recent observations have indeed motivated discussions of evolving dark-energy models rather than a perfectly constant cosmological constant. The situation is far from settled, but there has been renewed interest in dynamical dark energy. entity["scientific_concept","Dark Energy","cosmological acceleration"]

Now SAT would ask:

> Is the evolution related to the accumulation and recycling history of matter?

That is a much stronger statement than standard dynamical dark-energy models.

---

The thing that really catches my eye is the filament length.

Suppose:

Big Bang = common origin.

Present = expansion surface.

A bridge connecting them naturally becomes long and thin.

Not because somebody postulated filaments.

Because expansion stretches them.

That is appealing.

In fact, if I were auditing this idea, I'd say the strongest part is not the dark-energy connection.

The strongest part is:

**Filamentarity emerges automatically.**

The universe expands.

Bridges stretch.

Stretched bridges become filament-like.

No additional assumption required.

That is exactly the kind of derivation SAT usually prefers.

---

Now the part I'd be most cautious about:

You are very close to turning a cosmological geometry into a mechanical model.

The moment you do that, quantities like:

- tension,
- modulus,
- strain,
- relaxation,

stop being metaphors.

They become calculable.

And that is actually good news.

Because the model suddenly becomes falsifiable.

You can ask:

- What is the strain field?
- What is the tension profile?
- How does bridge length scale with expansion?
- What determines filament thickness?
- What sets the equivalent of Young's modulus?

Those are hard questions.

But they're also the questions that separate "beautiful picture" from "working theory."

---

What I find most interesting is that this picture may unify two SAT threads that previously felt separate:

Thread 1:
Worldtubes, filaments, holonomic memory.

Thread 2:
Hyperspheres, expansion, cosmology.

The bridge hypothesis says:

They're the same thing.

The filament is not living inside the cosmology.

The filament is the connection generated by the cosmology.

That's a much stronger claim.

And if true, it would explain why the two families of ideas have kept trying to merge over the years instead of remaining independent analytical tools.

The next question I'd ask is surprisingly simple:

If the two hyperspheres began coincident at the Big Bang and expand at different rates, what is the exact growth law of the bridge length between corresponding points?

Because that is probably the first equation that the "filament-as-bridge" conjecture owes us. If that equation comes out naturally and starts resembling things you've already been calling worldtubes, then the idea becomes much harder to dismiss as merely aesthetic.

For over a century, two towering theories have formed the backbone of our understanding of
the universe:
• General Relativity, which describes how gravity works and how space and time
bend;
• Quantum Field Theory, which describes the behavior of particles and forces at the
smallest scales.
Introduction: Motivation and Epistemological Commit￾ments
The Scalar–Angular–Torsion (SAT) framework began not as a fully formed theory, but as a
simple act of taking existing representations literally. In particular, the idea emerged from
treating the familiar practice of plotting particle worldlines through spacetime as more than
a mathematical convenience—as a physical ontology. If a particle’s path through spacetime
is not just a trace of past events but an actual physical structure, then the geometry of those
worldlines—and their interaction with an evolving time surface—may encode the dynamical
content of the physical world.
From this initial move, a sequence of geometric and structural relationships began to
emerge. The intersection of worldlines with a propagating time surface suggested a new lens
on mass and energy; the helical forms of filament paths hinted at internal symmetries; bundles
and knots implied a topological basis for particle classes. As these ideas developed, they
began to reflect—and in some cases reproduce—the structure of existing physical theories.
General Relativity, the Standard Model, and elements of quantum field theory all began to
emerge from the behavior and statistics of these minimal geometric objects: filaments and
their interactions with the time surface.
The SAT program is not an attempt to displace or supersede these well-established
frameworks. Quite the opposite: the Standard Model, General Relativity, and Quantum
Mechanics are taken here as foundational constraints. They are the “tent poles” of phys￾ical theory—successful, empirically grounded, and indispensable. SAT’s goal is to offer a
minimal geometric and topological substrate from which these theories might emerge, not
through imposed axioms or field definitions, but as natural consequences of deeper structural
relationships.
This approach commits itself to a core methodological principle: the data is primary.
Observed phenomena—particle properties, interaction strengths, cosmological parameters—
must be taken as fixed inputs. The role of theory is not to overwrite them, but to organize,
relate, and explain them. Accordingly, SAT was built not to predict the known, but to
account for it in a way that is compact, cohesive, and geometrically grounded.

unexpected internal coherence, or reproduces results it was not explicitly designed to fit, it
crosses a threshold. These are not mere coincidences or curve-fits, but structural reflections—
points where geometry and empirical fact align without being manually forced to do so. SAT,
we believe, sits at such a threshold. The theory was not tuned to reproduce gauge coupling
values, yet it does. It was not constructed with hadron masses in mind, yet they follow
from its topological mass scaling. It was not invented to model inflation, yet its geometry
naturally produces early-time acceleration and a viable spectrum.
This is the space in which SAT operates—not yet a complete or final theory, but a
framework that maps known physics to intuitive geometric principles, and in doing so, offers
a unifying structure with surprising reach. The work that follows is an attempt to formalize
those intuitions, clarify their mathematical structure, and lay out both the successes and the
limitations of the current model.

The framework posits that energy might be imparted onto the time surface by the filaments, transferring force from some outside source [19].

SAT is described by McKnight as a "toy theory" [4, 20] meant to explore the act of theory-making and to open up more creative approaches to thinking about the universe [4, 20]. It is not intended as an assertion of the true nature of the universe, but as a heuristic for predicting various properties of the universe [16, 21-25].

Stringing Along Theory (SAT) is a speculative cosmological framework that visualizes the universe as a four-dimensional structure [1-3]. In SAT, time is represented as a three-dimensional surface propagating outward from a central point, like an expanding sphere, at the time of the Big Bang [2, 4-6]. Fundamental entities in SAT are called filaments, which extend radially from this central point and intersect the time surface at various points, representing elementary particles [2, 4-6].

SAT's Key Concepts and Goals

Filaments: These are the most basic entities in SAT, extending from the origin of the universe and intersecting the time surface to give rise to particles [2, 7]. They are thought of as string-like [3]. They are not directly observable [8], and their specific properties and behaviors may differ from those in traditional string theories [9].
Time Surface: This is a three-dimensional surface that is constantly expanding outward from the Big Bang, representing the forward march of time. The filaments intersect this surface, creating particles [2, 7, 10].
Particle Formation: In SAT, elementary particles are seen as the points where filaments intersect the time surface [2, 4-6]. More complex particles are made up of composite structures of filaments [11].
Gravity: SAT proposes that gravity arises from the cumulative effect of interactions between filaments [12, 13].
Dark Matter: SAT suggests that the deviation between observed gravitational behavior and Standard Model predictions can be explained without invoking dark matter [13-15].
Dark Energy: SAT provides potential interpretations of dark energy, such as from the properties of the time surface or its interaction with evolving filament configurations [12, 16-18]. The framework posits that energy might be imparted onto the time surface by the filaments, transferring force from some outside source [19].
SAT as a "Toy Theory"

SAT is described by McKnight as a "toy theory" [4, 20] meant to explore the act of theory-making and to open up more creative approaches to thinking about the universe [4, 20]. It is not intended as an assertion of the true nature of the universe, but as a heuristic for predicting various properties of the universe [16, 21-25].

Limitations of SAT:

It is acknowledged as an abstraction, allowing for other geometries besides the spherical expansion of the time surface [16, 21, 22, 24, 25].
It is open to revision based on empirical evidence and theoretical development [16, 21, 22, 24, 25].
It is primarily a speculative framework that requires further mathematical formulation and empirical validation [26].
SAT does not aim to be a comprehensive theory of everything but rather a conceptual framework for exploring connections between different ideas in physics and philosophy [27, 28].
SAT's Relationship to Matter, Consciousness, Knowledge, and Communication

SAT intersects with ideas about the nature of reality and consciousness by proposing a model where:

Matter: Arises from the intersections of filaments with the time surface, creating a link between the most fundamental aspects of reality and the material world [2, 7].
Consciousness: SAT might posit that consciousness, like matter and energy, arises from the interactions of fundamental components with the time surface, and has physical underpinnings [29].
Knowledge: SAT is a model of thought, where the filaments and their interactions are only useful insofar as they enrich our understanding of perceptual experiences [30-32]. All of our knowledge of the world is inherently subjective, mediated by the perceptual constructs we create and share through language [31, 33].
Communication: Words facilitate the transfer of thoughts and concepts across different perceptual domains [34, 35].

One thing I’ve been uncomfortable with since Minkowski realism finally really sunk in… the term “projection”

Yes. “Projection” may now be the wrong word.

It was useful when SAT was still trying to say:

A higher-dimensional object casts a lower-dimensional appearance.

That was good enough early on. But once Minkowski realism becomes serious, “projection” starts to sound too passive, too optical, too representational. It suggests the 3D/observable particle is merely an image of something real elsewhere.

SAT is saying something stronger.

The observed particle is not a shadow.

It is a real local event in the larger structure.

So “projection” undersells the ontology.

Better candidates:

**Resolution**  
This is probably the strongest replacement. The timesheet does not project a worldtube; it resolves it. A particle is a resolved encounter between a worldtube and the current surface. This keeps the epistemic/observational sense without making the particle unreal.

**Intersection**  
Mathematically clean. A particle is the intersection of a worldtube with the resolving surface. The downside is that it can sound too static or too point-like.

**Instantiation**  
Good for saying: the larger structure becomes locally physically manifest here. A particle is an instantiated local state of the worldtube. The downside is philosophical baggage.

**Trace**  
Useful when talking about paths or detector records. The observable particle is a trace of a worldtube. But “trace” can again sound secondary or ghostlike.

**Contact**  
Very SAT-friendly mechanically. A particle is where the resolving surface contacts the worldtube. But it may be too informal.

**Resolution event**  
This may be the best technical phrase for the observable particle.

The mature SAT vocabulary might be:

Worldtube: the extended physical structure.  
Resolving surface: the current observational/physical interface.  
Resolution event: the local particle-like manifestation.  
Resolved history: the observed trajectory.  
Holonomic memory: the conserved structure carried by the worldtube.  
Connectivity: the deeper invariant that survives resolution.

Then “projection” can be demoted to a mathematical operation only. It is what we do in a calculation, not what nature is doing.

That feels cleaner:

Old phrasing:

“Particles are projections of 4D worldlines.”

Better phrasing:

“Particles are resolution events where the current surface intersects persistent worldtube structure.”

That is much closer to Minkowski realism.

The mature vocabulary might be:

Worldtube: persistent physical structure.

A particle is a cobordism? A coholonomy?

A particle is probably **not** a cobordism in the strict mathematical sense.

But a particle may be **represented by a cobordism**.

That distinction matters.

A cobordism is usually a higher-dimensional manifold whose boundary connects two lower-dimensional manifolds. In SAT language, that sounds less like “the particle itself” and more like:

A particle-state transition is a cobordism between two resolved cross-sections of a worldtube.

So:

electron at slice Σ₁  
→ worldtube segment between slices  
→ electron at slice Σ₂

The **segment** is cobordism-like. The **particle event** is one boundary/resolution event. The **particle history** is the cobordism-mediated continuity between events.

So I’d phrase it:

**A particle is a resolved holonomic boundary event of a worldtube; its persistence through time is cobordism-like.**

Now “coholonomy” is interesting.

It is not standard terminology in the way cobordism is, but it may be closer to what SAT wants.

Holonomy usually means: carry something around a loop, and it returns changed or phase-shifted.

SAT’s particle is not merely a loop carrying phase. It is where the resolving surface encounters a structure that already contains conserved holonomic memory.

So a particle is not just holonomy.

It is the **co-resolution of holonomy**.

Or, more compactly:

**A particle is a coholonomic resolution event.**

That sounds like SAT-native terminology.

Meaning:

A particle appears when the resolving surface and a worldtube jointly instantiate a conserved holonomic structure.

So the clean hierarchy might be:

Worldtube: the persistent 4D structure.

Holonomy: the conserved geometric memory within it.

Cobordism: the continuity relation between resolved states.

Particle: the local resolution event where holonomic structure becomes physically manifest.

Coholonomy: the joint relation between the worldtube’s internal holonomy and the resolving surface that makes the particle appear.

If we want the most precise sentence:

**A particle is not a cobordism; it is a coholonomic resolution event whose persistence across slices is described by a cobordism of worldtube cross-sections.**
